node.label: Tandem
node.summary: An AI study planner that turns your syllabus and deadlines into a realistic weekly plan, then adapts when life happens.

node.label: Price-conscious trialists
node.summary: Students who will try new tools if a real free tier exists, but cancel subscriptions often and compare against free apps. The evidence points to widespread subscription fatigue and a strong pull toward free student app lists.

node.label: Time-starved students juggling commitments
node.summary: Students with unstable schedules, such as those balancing jobs and coursework. They value hours saved over price. Planning research suggests the people who gain most from planning are those facing interruptions.

node.label: Entrenched Notion / all-in-one users
node.summary: Students who have built their systems in Notion or similar workspaces. They will only switch if it is painless. Some show fatigue with complexity and interest in alternatives.

node.label: Group-chat-driven adopters
node.summary: Students who adopt tools their friend groups already use. Peer vouching outweighs features. This segment is the core of word-of-mouth and short-form social spread.

node.label: Institution-guided new students
node.summary: First-year students steered toward university-provided apps and digital planners, plus back-to-school planner roundups. They default to free, officially endorsed tools.

node.label: Subscription fatigue
node.summary: Productivity subscriptions are widely seen as too expensive. Students cancel periodically and gravitate to mostly free tools.

node.label: Painful switching from existing systems
node.summary: Long-time users of incumbent workspaces need near-effortless migration before they will switch.

node.label: All-in-one tools are overly complicated
node.summary: Feature-packed second-brain apps are described as overly complicated. Many abandon them after investing time in setup.

node.label: Plans break when schedules are disrupted
node.summary: Interruptions and unstable schedules undermine plans. Planning support helps most where life is unpredictable.

node.label: Deadline and finals crunch
node.summary: Campuses run structured study-session programmes for finals. This shows recurring difficulty managing workload around deadlines.

node.label: Concerns about data control and privacy
node.summary: Recurring coverage of privacy-focused and local-first alternatives reflects unease about cloud-held personal data.

node.label: Desire to save hours each week
node.summary: For time-pressed students, a tool that clearly saves time makes price secondary.

node.label: Desire for a genuine free tier
node.summary: Willingness to try new tools depends on a meaningful free option.

node.label: Desire for peer-vouched tools
node.summary: Adoption is triggered when friends already use and recommend a tool.

node.label: Back-to-school planner and organisation demand
node.summary: There is seasonal coverage of student planners, calendar apps and organisation tips around the start of term.

node.label: Search for Notion alternatives
node.summary: Many articles cover privacy-focused, open-source and local-first replacements for Notion.

node.label: Second-brain fatigue and simplification
node.summary: Users are abandoning complex productivity systems for simpler tools.

node.label: Subscription backlash
node.summary: People are shifting away from paid productivity apps toward mostly free tools, and price creep is a reported driver of switching.

node.label: Universities providing digital planners
node.summary: Universities are partnering with big tech or shipping official apps for student organisation.

node.label: AI embedded in productivity tools
node.summary: Workspaces and alternatives are adding AI-powered automation and documentation features.

node.label: Notion
node.summary: Dominant all-in-one workspace that many consolidate apps into. It has AI integration but is criticised as overly complicated, and it faces a steady stream of alternatives over privacy and data-control concerns.

node.label: MyStudyLife
node.summary: Free student-specific planner, the kind of tool that appears in student calendar and organisation app roundups. There is no direct evidence on its position.

node.label: ChatGPT
node.summary: General AI assistant. Students could improvise plans with it, and AI features are increasingly embedded in productivity tools. There is no direct student-planning evidence for it.

node.label: Todoist
node.summary: Task manager of the kind featured in free and time-management app lists for students. The evidence does not show it adapting plans to syllabi.

node.label: Free tools
node.summary: Free student apps and mostly free productivity tools are the default comparison.

event.question: In your own words, what is this product and who is it for?
event.answer: It's an AI study planner where you upload your syllabus and deadlines and it builds you a weekly plan that's actually doable. When you miss a day or something comes up, it reshuffles everything. It's for uni students like me who get buried around midterms and finals.

event.question: Walk me through how you decided what to do about it.
event.answer: Gia and Iris both saw the demo and kept bringing up how it re-plans your week when life happens, so it got on my radar. I don't switch tools much, so I'm waiting to see if more people in the group chat actually start using it, not just watch a demo. If a couple of them are still on it after a few weeks, I'll probably try it before finals.

event.question: What bothers you about it, or would stop you from using it?
event.answer: I'm worried it's a cool demo that I'd stop opening after two weeks, like every planner I've downloaded. I'm also not sure it does enough more than asking ChatGPT for a schedule or using the free planners people already have. Another $8 subscription adds up on a student budget, and if my friends drop it I probably would too.

event.question: What would you realistically pay, and why that number?
event.answer: Probably around $5 a month, or $8 only if there's a student discount or a cheaper yearly plan. $8 isn't crazy, but it's close to what I pay for Spotify, and that feels like a lot for a planner I might only lean on hard during crunch weeks. A free trial that covers a real deadline week would help a lot.

event.question: Where would you expect to hear about something like this, and what message would convince you?
event.answer: Honestly the group chat first, then maybe TikTok if someone shows their actual week getting rescheduled. What would convince me is a friend saying they used it through midterms and didn't fall behind. Ads saying 'AI-powered' don't really do anything for me.

event.question: Would you recommend it to a friend? What exactly would you tell them?
event.answer: Not yet, since I haven't used it myself. If it worked, I'd tell them it's the planner that fixes your schedule when you fall behind, so you don't have to redo everything at 2am. I'd also tell them to try it during a heavy week to see if it's worth the $8.

event.question: What would you realistically pay, and why that number?
